newsitem.title: USA: CAW target decision sets up GM showdown with UAW.
newsitem.headline: CAW target decision sets up GM showdown with UAW.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers' decision on Monday to bargain next with General Motors Corp. suggests the United Auto Workers will now move on to Chrysler Corp. and save tough job security issues at GM for last.
If that is the case, it could set up a fall showdown between the UAW and GM, the world's largest automaker, that some analysts fear could end up in a strike.
"The word I'm trying to get out to suppliers is be prepared," said Donna Parolini, whose Troy, Mich.-based International Business Development Corp. consults with auto suppliers.

UAW officials have not notified Chrysler or GM which company will be the second bargaining target, representatives of both automakers said Monday. A union spokesman said a decision on which company would be next has not been made.
But CAW President Buzz Hargrove said Monday he is certain UAW President Steve Yokich will not pick GM next.

"We have a clear understanding between myself and Mr. Yokich of the UAW that we will not do anything to interfere or harm one another in our efforts to put together a 1996 collective agreement," he said.

The UAW, which represents nearly 400,000 hourly auto workers in the United States, last week reached a tentative agreement with Ford Motor Co.. The union typically gets an agreement with one of Detroit's Big Three and then applies those terms as a pattern to the remaining two.

The UAW's three-year pact with all automakers expired Sept. 14. The union extended the deadline at Chrysler and GM while it negotiated at Ford. But in a break with tradition, Yokich has continued subcommittee discussions at Chrysler and GM. It is possible, analysts have said, that Yokich will continue to talk with remaining two simultaneously.

Analysts said GM and the UAW will have the most trouble reaching a new labour accord because union job security concerns clash directly with the company's determined efforts to sell unprofitable parts plants and reduce headcount.
That view was reinforced by the Ford-UAW deal, which guarantees the company will keep 95 percent of its UAW hourly workers through the three-year agreement, unless a severe market downturn occurs.
"The real reason you push GM to last is they have the most difficult issues," said Paul Ballew, chief economist in the Troy, Mich., office of industry consultant J.D. Power and Associates.

An independent study by Harbour & Associates released last May concluded GM needed to shed about 33,000 workers from its assembly, stamping and powertrain operations to reach the productivity levels of Ford and Chrysler.

Ballew, like other industry analysts, also believes GM and the CAW could be headed for a strike. Chrysler, in a deal reached last week with CAW bargainers, promised to add jobs, increase wages and replace any job that it contracts out with a similar job at one of its Canadian plants.

Analysts said there is no way GM can accept those terms. For that reason, GM executives are evaluating how to stockpile parts and best brace for a strike in Canada, Parolini of International Business Development said.

GM spokesman Tom Klipstine said the automaker's assembly operations are still trying to recoup light vehicle supplies lost during the Dayton, Ohio, strike in March that crippled North American production. He said the company is not building up inventory to brace for a strike.
"We basically have been in a position of playing catch-up," he said.
